content.audience_tension: The target audience — urban professionals aged 25-40 who make coffee at home and say they value ritual over convenience — live inside schedules built for speed. For most of that group, coffee on a weekday is something you get (a pod, a drip machine on autopilot, a coffee-shop stop) rather than something you make. The tension is between wanting mornings to feel intentional and self-directed, and defaulting to whatever costs the least time, because deliberately slowing down can feel indulgent or impractical on a Tuesday. The brief names this tension directly by setting 'ritual' against 'convenience' as competing values, by pricing the product at $38 (a considered purchase, not an impulse one), and by warning against generic luxury imagery — the tension is not 'I want to look rich,' it's 'I want five minutes that are mine before the day takes them.'
content.desired_behavior: A viewer sees the :15 vertical video or one of the two 4:5 stills on social, recognizes the five-minute pour-over moment as a version of a morning ritual they want for themselves (not as an ad for 'a kitchen gadget'), and takes a direct-response action: clicks through to the Solace DTC site and adds the $38 pour-over dripper to cart. The objective is explicitly DTC visits and add-to-carts, not brand-awareness alone, so the creative must carry a clear, low-friction path from feeling to action.
content.product_relevance: The ceramic pour-over cannot be a backdrop prop for a generic 'calm morning' mood — it has to be the literal mechanism that makes the ritual happen: the user stands at it, pours, waits, watches the water bloom the grounds. Its three verified attributes reinforce that role rather than sit apart from it: hand-glazed stoneware and small-batch production make the object itself read as considered and singular (supporting 'ritual', not 'appliance'), while dishwasher-safe care keeps the ritual repeatable on an ordinary Tuesday rather than precious or occasional. This is how the strategy satisfies the brief's required 'clear product role in the story' and 'readable closing product moment' without leaning on unverified performance claims (e.g., taste, extraction quality, temperature control) that were not supplied as facts.
content.single_minded_proposition: The Solace pour-over is the five hands-on minutes you take back for yourself before the day takes the rest of your time — a small, repeatable act of choosing slow on purpose. (This operationalizes the brief's own key message, 'A five-minute ritual that slows your morning down, on purpose,' as a proposition the creative director can build routes against.)
proof_points: Hand-glazed stoneware ceramic (verified fact): each piece carries visible handmade variation, giving the object a tactile, one-of-a-kind quality that a mass-produced plastic or metal drip gadget cannot claim — supports 'ritual object' over 'kitchen appliance.'

Made in small batches (verified fact): reinforces a considered, non-commodity positioning consistent with a $38 price point and with the brief's instruction to avoid generic luxury imagery — the claim to make is 'made with care in limited runs,' not 'exclusive' or 'luxury.'

Dishwasher safe (verified fact): removes the plausible objection that a 'ritual' object is too precious or high-maintenance to use every weekday — the ritual survives real life, which is what makes it repeatable rather than a one-time novelty.

Structural (not brand-specific) pour-over mechanic: manual pour-over brewing requires the user's continuous attention for several minutes, unlike a pod or programmable drip machine — this is a general characteristic of the pour-over method and is treated here as a category fact, not a tested claim about the Solace product's performance, taste, or extraction quality.
success_criteria: Increase in click-throughs from the campaign's video and still placements to the Solace DTC product page, among the stated home-coffee-enthusiast audience segment.
Add-to-cart rate on site visits attributed to this campaign's creative, tracked against the campaign's own traffic (not an invented industry benchmark, since no baseline was supplied).

Qualitative signal that the 'ritual, on purpose' message is landing as intended — e.g., audience comments, saves, or shares that reference slowing down / morning ritual language rather than generic product-feature language.

Creative compliance checks the strategist can hand to the creative director and QC: every route keeps a clear, legible product role in the story and a readable closing product moment (both explicit brief requirements), and makes no performance, taste, or research claim beyond the three verified facts.

Note: no numeric targets (specific CTR%, add-to-cart %, conversion rate) are set here, because the brief and upstream context supplied no baseline or target figures; these should be defined by the producer/brand with actual analytics before being used as pass/fail thresholds.

routes.central_idea: Before the phone, the inbox, or anyone else gets a piece of you, there are five minutes that are only yours — marked by the pour.
routes.emotional_promise: Quiet self-possession: the felt relief of claiming a few minutes before the day starts claiming them for you.
routes.product_role: The Solace dripper is the literal boundary object. The film's one deliberate action — setting the phone face-down and reaching for the dripper instead — makes the product the mechanism of the choice, not a backdrop to it. It stays in frame through the pour, the bloom, and the final held mug, closing on an unhurried, fully lit shot of the dripper itself on the counter.
routes.visual_language: Quiet and continuous, no contrast-cutting: warm low window light, muted stoneware palette (terracotta, cream, soft grey), handheld-but-steady camera, close but not macro. Sound carries more of the emotion than music — water, steam, ceramic set down, a phone buzzing once, off-screen and ignored.
routes.execution_example: 15s / 9:16 (D01): Open tight on a phone screen lighting up on a counter; a hand turns it face-down without looking. Cut to the same hand lifting the Solace dripper, setting it on a mug, spooning grounds. Slow spiral pour, water blooming the grounds in close-up (2-3s held). Cut to the person at a window, mug in both hands, steam rising, a single distant notification sound goes unanswered. Final beat (2s): dripper alone on the counter in soft full light, product fully legible, with an illustrative closing line such as 'Made in small batches' (exact copy owned by copywriter). The two 4:5 stills (D02) pull directly from this beat structure: still 1 = the pour/bloom close-up with the dripper as clear hero object; still 2 = the closing counter shot, product fully visible and legible, doubling as a clean DTC-linkable product image.

routes.central_idea: The bloom itself — the moment water first meets the grounds — is the ritual's whole point, and the hand-glazed ceramic is filmed as the singular object that stages it.
routes.emotional_promise: Presence: the satisfaction of doing one small thing slowly enough to actually notice it happening.
routes.product_role: The dripper's surface and form are the visual subject, not just present in the shot. Macro texture on the hand-glazed stoneware (visible glaze variation, no two pieces identical) is used to make the tactile, handmade proof point legible on screen, then the frame pulls back to show the object in full use — giving the product both an intimate role and a clear closing moment.
routes.visual_language: Macro and shallow depth of field, slow motion on water contact and steam, warm directional morning light, near-silent sound design (pour, drip, a single ceramic clink) with minimal or no music. No other objects compete in frame — discipline here is what keeps it from reading as generic 'luxury lifestyle' imagery.
routes.execution_example: 15s / 9:16 (D01): Near-entirely macro — dry grounds catching light, first pour, the bloom rising and settling, steam curling off the surface, a fingertip resting briefly on the glaze's texture. In the last 3 seconds, camera pulls back for the first time to a clean, fully lit shot of the dripper and finished mug on the counter, with a hand entering frame to lift the mug — the human presence and the product both land together as the closing moment. Illustrative closing line: 'Hand-glazed. Small batch. Yours.' The two 4:5 stills (D02) isolate: still 1 = the bloom macro shot; still 2 = the pulled-back closing counter shot, framed as a clean product/DTC image.

routes.central_idea: An ordinary Tuesday, not a weekend — the deliberate choice to reach for the slow thing instead of the fast thing, on a day that gave no permission to slow down.
routes.emotional_promise: Quiet agency: permission to choose slowness even when nothing about the day is asking for it.
routes.product_role: The dripper is staged as the chosen alternative in an explicit two-beat decision (reach for the fast option, then don't — reach for this instead), which makes its role in the story unmissable. It remains the visual anchor through the pour and into a final in-focus product shot.
routes.visual_language: Two-beat structure with a movement contrast rather than a lighting contrast (to avoid a glossy before/after ad feel): a slightly quicker, handheld beat for the 'fast' cue, settling into a locked-off, steady frame for the pour. Same muted warm palette throughout so the shift feels like a change in pace, not a change in world.
routes.execution_example: 15s / 9:16 (D01): Opens on an out-of-focus stack of notifications/alarm on a phone, a hand starting to reach for it — then redirects to the Solace dripper sitting on the counter instead. One continuous, steady pour; the frame holds on the bloom. Final beat: person seated, mug in both hands, dripper still visible in soft foreground focus. On-screen line (illustrative, copywriter to finalize): 'A five-minute ritual, on purpose.' The two 4:5 stills (D02): still 1 = the redirected-hand moment (phone out of focus behind, dripper sharp in the foreground) carrying the tension itself; still 2 = the seated closing shot with the product legible in frame.

content.recommendation_rationale: R1 ("the line before the day") most directly dramatizes the strategy's own audience tension — ritual vs. the pull of convenience — through one specific, small, believable action (turning the phone face-down) rather than a generic mood board or an explicit before/after contrast edit. That keeps it furthest from the brief's 'generic luxury imagery without a story' risk while still giving the product an unambiguous role and a clean, legible closing shot that doubles easily as a DTC-linkable image. Its single continuous pace (no hard tonal cut) also fits the brief's 'quiet, warm, tactile' tone more precisely than R3's two-beat contrast, and it extends more naturally to both required still crops than R2's mostly-macro treatment, which risks losing legible product context if used as a static image on its own. R2 and R3 remain strong alternates: R2 is the more sensory, tactile-proof-point-forward option if the brand wants to foreground the hand-glazed/small-batch facts even more literally; R3 is the more literal, message-forward option if the producer wants the 'on purpose' contrast made explicit rather than implied.

story.logline: At 7:00 a.m. NORA turns her buzzing phone face-down and reaches for the Solace dripper instead, and until 7:05 the day gets nothing from her.

beat_sheet.heading: INT. NORA'S KITCHEN - COUNTER - 7:00 AM
beat_sheet.what_happens: Her phone lights up with 7:00 on the screen and buzzes on the counter. NORA flips it face-down without looking, lifts the Solace dripper off the dish rack, seats it on her chipped mug and presses a folded paper filter into the cone.
beat_sheet.turn: The day's first demand is refused, and the hand that refused it goes to the dripper. Her five minutes start here, at 7:00.

beat_sheet.heading: INT. NORA'S KITCHEN - COUNTER - CONTINUOUS
beat_sheet.what_happens: Cut to grounds already heaped in the filter. She pours a slow spiral from the kettle, and the grounds swell and dome up inside the dripper. Nothing else happens in frame.
beat_sheet.turn: The five minutes began at 7:00 with the flip, and the pour is what fills them. The frame now belongs to the ritual, not the phone.

beat_sheet.heading: INT. NORA'S KITCHEN - COUNTER - MOMENTS LATER
beat_sheet.what_happens: A last drip falls as she lifts the dripper off the mug and sets it down beside the face-down phone. The phone lights up again, and its glow leaks out around the edges onto the wood as it rattles. Her hand stays on the mug until the glow dies. Card: 'Everyone else gets you at 7:05.'
beat_sheet.turn: The second demand gets nothing either, and the card says when it will: 7:05. The boundary holds, and the dripper is what drew it.

beat_sheet.heading: INT. NORA'S KITCHEN - COUNTER - MOMENTS LATER
beat_sheet.what_happens: The mug is gone. The Solace dripper stands empty on the counter, whole and legible, and the phone is still face-down and dark at the edge of frame. The verified facts come on screen, then the CTA.
beat_sheet.turn: She took the coffee and left the phone. The tool becomes the hero, and the viewer is told where to buy one.

deliverable_scripts.idea_in_one_line: The pour is the boundary: at 7:00 the phone goes face-down and the dripper comes up, and nobody gets her until 7:05.

beats.picture: HOOK. A phone lies face-up on a wooden counter beside a dish rack. Its generic lock screen lights up with 7:00 in large digits, readable, and it buzzes. At about 0.8s NORA's hand comes into frame, flips the phone face-down without her looking, and keeps moving toward the dish rack.
beats.sound: Phone buzz rattling on wood, then the flat clack of glass landing face-down. Then silence.

beats.picture: The same hand lifts the Solace dripper off the dish rack, seats it on a chipped white mug, and presses a folded paper filter down into the cone.
beats.sound: Stoneware clicking onto the mug rim; the dry crinkle of the paper filter pressed into the cone.
beats.on_screen_text: Nobody gets you before the pour.

beats.picture: Cut to grounds already heaped in the filter. NORA's hand tips a gooseneck kettle and pours a slow spiral onto them. The grounds swell, bubble and dome up against the paper inside the dripper. Hold on the bloom.
beats.sound: Thin stream of water on wet grounds; the soft fizz of the bloom. No music.

beats.picture: NORA's hand lifts the Solace dripper off the chipped mug, a last drip falling from its tip into the coffee, and sets it down on the wooden counter beside the face-down phone.
beats.sound: A last drip plinking into the coffee; stoneware set down on wood.

beats.picture: The face-down phone lights up, and a glow leaks out around its edges onto the wood as it rattles. Beside it, NORA's hand wraps around the chipped mug and stays there until the glow dies.
beats.sound: One phone buzz rattling against the wood, left unanswered. It stops. Room tone.

beats.picture: Moments later, with the mug and hand gone, the Solace dripper stands empty on the wooden counter with its filter out, and its glaze has pooled unevenly at the foot. At the frame edge, clear of the dripper, the phone lies face-down and dark. The whole product is in frame and legible.
beats.sound: Room tone; the kettle ticking as it cools off-screen.
beats.on_screen_text: Hand-glazed stoneware. Made in small batches.

beats.picture: Same picture as B5, held: the empty Solace dripper on the wooden counter with its glaze pooled unevenly at the foot, and the phone face-down and dark at the frame edge. The whole product is legible. Nothing in frame moves.
beats.sound: Room tone and the kettle ticking as it cools, to the last frame. No music, no sting.
beats.on_screen_text: Shop the Solace dripper. Link in bio.

decisions.choice: A deliberate break from the route's execution example: the window-and-mug shot is cut. In its place (B4b), the face-down phone lights up a second time, its glow leaking around the edges onto the wood as it rattles, and NORA's hand stays on the mug until the glow dies.
decisions.reason: The window shot is the first thing the taste notes reject. The replacement keeps R1's idea and the product's role. With the sound off, the second refusal reads from the edge glow and the 7:05 card. With the sound on, the rattle lands alone in room tone. This corrects the last version, which relied on the phone creeping a few millimetres, and that would not show on a phone screen.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Anyone gazing out a window holding a mug' (reject); Craft brief: 'The story must read from picture and on-screen text alone'; Route R1 product_role

decisions.choice: NORA appears only as hands and forearms. No face appears in the spot or in either still.
decisions.reason: Her hands carry the story: flip, lift, filter, pour, set down, hold. A face would push the spot toward stock lifestyle footage.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Hands before faces'; Craft brief: stock-lifestyle picture rejects

decisions.choice: The hook is the phone flip. The lock screen's 7:00 is readable for about 0.8s before NORA's hand arrives, and the flip is complete by 1.5s. There is no VO and no card over it.
decisions.reason: It is a specific action in the first frame and the route's one deliberate choice. A readable 7:00 sets up the 7:05 card, so the clock works for people watching muted.
decisions.source: Craft brief: hook rule; Route R1 execution example; reviewer note 1

decisions.choice: The spot has no VO: 0 spoken words in 15s. The 7:00-to-7:05 idea moves to the B4b card, 'Everyone else gets you at 7:05.' (6 words), which bookends the B2 card 'Nobody gets you before the pour.' 'Five minutes, on purpose.' now appears only on still 2.
decisions.reason: The last version's line ('Everyone else can have you at seven-oh-five') was 9 spoken words in a 3.5s beat, about 2.6 per second. It also ran over the buzz that is the story's turn, and only people with the sound on got the payoff. As a card it reaches muted viewers, and the buzz lands on its own. The open still runs 7.5s with no VO, as before.
decisions.source: Craft brief: timing budget and sound-off rule; Taste notes: 'Restraint over explanation', 'Dry over sentimental'; reviewer note 1

decisions.choice: The old B4 is split into B4a (7.5-9.0s: the dripper is lifted off the mug and set down) and B4b (9.0-11.0s: the second buzz, the hand staying on the mug, the 7:05 card). B5 and B6 keep their IDs, so the review notes still point to the right beats.
decisions.reason: One action per beat. The old 3.5s beat carried four actions, a card and a VO. Now the buzz and the card that answers it get 2s to themselves.
decisions.source: Reviewer note 1; Craft brief: 'one card per roughly 2 seconds'

decisions.choice: B2 ends with a folded paper filter pressed into the cone, and B3 opens on grounds already heaped in it. The spooning happens in the cut.
decisions.reason: This fixes the filter that was never put in. Lifting, seating and filtering fit into 2.5s; adding the spoon did not.
decisions.source: Reviewer note 3; Quality bar: continuity that holds, nothing physically implausible

decisions.choice: No music at all. Real sounds carry the mood: the buzz rattling on wood, the flat clack of glass landing face-down, stoneware clicking onto the mug rim, the filter crinkle, the kettle stream, the bloom fizz, the last drip, stoneware on wood, and the kettle ticking as it cools.
decisions.reason: The taste notes allow music 'late, if at all'. Leaving it out keeps the second buzz audible, and that buzz is the turn.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Sound design before music'; Route R1 visual_language

decisions.choice: The product works as a tool in B2 to B4a (lifted, poured through, set down) and becomes the hero in B5 to B6 (4s in total). New timing: B5 (11.0-12.5s) holds the product with the facts card for 1.5s before the CTA, and B6 (12.5-15.0s) gives the CTA 2.5s, the longest any card is on screen.
decisions.reason: This meets both must-includes and the craft brief's 1.5s minimum product hold. It also gives the line that drives conversion the most reading time.
decisions.source: Brief must-include; Craft brief: product moment; Taste notes: 'The product is a tool, then a hero'; Brief objective: DTC visits and add-to-carts; reviewer note 5

decisions.choice: In B5 and B6 the mug is gone, and the phone is still face-down and dark at the edge of frame, clear of the dripper: she took the coffee and left the phone. Still 2 drops the phone so it works as a clean product image.
decisions.reason: The packshot keeps the idea on screen until the CTA, so the last 4 seconds belong to this route and not to just any ceramic cone. The dripper stays dominant and legible.
decisions.source: Route R1 product_role: 'the literal boundary object'; Quality bar: ending with no idea attached; Taste notes: ending reject; reviewer note 4

decisions.choice: The coffee drip on the outer glaze is cut from B5, B6 and still 2. The glaze pooled unevenly at the foot and the kettle ticking as it cools carry the hold.
decisions.reason: With the filter out, nothing could put coffee there, and on the DTC image it would read as a dripper that spills.

decisions.choice: Only three facts are stated: 'Hand-glazed stoneware' and 'Made in small batches' on the B5 card and still 1, and dishwasher safe on still 2 only, as 'it still goes in the dishwasher'. The pooled glaze shows the hand-glazing in the picture. Nothing is said about taste, speed or quality, and the price stays off screen.
decisions.reason: Only verified facts may be stated. The dishwasher line turns a spec into a dry, human line.
decisions.source: Brief: verified product facts; must avoid 'Unsupported performance claims'

decisions.choice: The CTA 'Shop the Solace dripper. Link in bio.' runs over the product frame. There is no logo-on-colour end card.
decisions.reason: It is a specific verb plus a destination, which serves DTC visits and add-to-carts. An ending with only a logo is a taste reject.
decisions.source: Craft brief: CTA rule; Taste notes: ending reject; Brief objective

decisions.choice: Each scene has one real detail: the dripper lives on the dish rack, the chipped white mug, and the phone left face-down after she has gone.
decisions.reason: Each makes the kitchen lived-in rather than generic luxury, and each does a job in the story.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'One real detail per scene', 'Real kitchens have a dish rack'; Brief must-avoid: generic luxury imagery

decisions.choice: All cards and still copy sit in negative space and never over the dripper. On still 1, copy stays clear of the dripper, the kettle and the pour, and design decides the exact placement.
decisions.reason: The product stays legible in every frame it appears in, and the pour stays uncovered.
decisions.source: Craft brief: on-screen text rule; reviewer note 5

assumptions: The product is called 'the Solace dripper', following the route. The brief only says 'ceramic pour-over', so the name must be confirmed before the end card and still sublines are locked.

'Five minutes', '7:00' and '7:05' frame the approved key message ('A five-minute ritual...'). They are not a measured brew-time claim. If legal reads them as a performance claim, the fallbacks are ready: B4b card becomes 'Everyone else can have you later.' (6 words) and the still 2 headline becomes 'On purpose.'
The B1 lock screen shows 7:00 so that the B4b 7:05 card pays off. The lock screen is a generic mock-up (see the rights items below).

characters.role_in_story: Principal and the only person in the cast. She appears as hands and forearms only. Her habit: every weekday at 7:00 she makes the pour before anyone else gets any of her. Objective: get the coffee poured and her hand around the mug while the phone gets nothing back from her. At B1 she turns it face-down and never turns it back. At B4b she doesn't touch it. She appears in D01-B1 to B4b and in D02-1. D01-B5, B6 and D02-2 have no person in them. The script sets the name and gender (NORA, she). Playing age is 33-39, target 36. That is a choice, not a story need: it sits inside the 25-40 audience and is old enough for the habit to look long-standing. Her age shows in knuckle creases, tendons and veins. I break two defaults on purpose. The category's default hand is late-20s, pale and slim, with a gloss manicure and stacked gold rings on a linen cuff. The generator's stock hand is long, tapered, poreless and light-skinned. The taste note 'Hands before faces' only works if the hand isn't stock, and breaking both also keeps us clear of the brief's must-avoid on generic luxury imagery. Heritage is South Asian American. It is recorded for continuity and kept out of the prompt, and with no face on screen it shows only as skin hex and texture. She has one mark from her life: a writer's callus on her right middle finger, from years of writing by hand. She still keeps her lists on paper rather than in the phone. This is backstory only and adds no prop, scene or copy. It puts the audience's 'ritual over convenience' into a single mark (taste note: 'one real detail... that only this place or person would have'). She is not presented as a customer or an expert, and there is no testimonial.
characters.screen_presence: One-frame read: a hand in its mid-thirties, with creased knuckles, short bare nails, a writer's callus and a mole on the back. It flattens a buzzing phone face-down on the first try and is already moving on toward the dish rack, so the flip reads as habit, not as someone acting calm. The hand never searches or hovers. It lands on an object, takes it and lets go. She lifts the dripper off the rack the way she'd lift a mug she uses every day, not like a presented object. During the pour her forearm stays still and only her wrist circles. Between actions her hands stop completely: flat, no tapping.
characters.performance_style: Understated. Silent: no dialogue, no lip-sync, no VO. No face is cast. At rest her hand lies flat and does nothing. Every move plays at the real-time pace of a daily habit, so there is no slow motion (taste reject). The flip is one continuous move of about 0.4 s that carries straight into the reach. Her one change comes at B4b: as the phone lights, her thumb slides once across the chip on the mug rim, over about half a second, and settles on it until the glow dies. The refusal plays as choosing the mug. Her hand never moves toward the phone, and her grip on the mug doesn't tighten.
characters.wardrobe_fit_notes: Height 167 cm (range 165-169). She is the only principal, so there is no one to scale against. Medium build, shoulders level with the hips, forearms as in the anchors. Right-handed. The mole and callus are on the right hand, and the director decides which hand does what in each shot. Hand: about 18 cm long and 8.5 cm across the knuckles. Product-scale constraint: in a one-hand grip on the dripper (B2, B4a), glaze must show on both sides of her hand. Her 8.5 cm knuckle breadth must therefore be at least 2 cm less than the rim diameter, which is pending from the client. If the rim is under 10.5 cm, the hand spec comes back to casting. Sleeves end at least 5 cm above the wrist bone on both arms, so no cuff crosses the dripper or the pour. Nothing on the fingers or wrists: a ring or watch would click on stoneware over the designed sound, and a watch would add a second clock against the story's 7:00 and 7:05. The sleeve colour must differ in value from both the skin (#6F4A34) and the dripper glaze, so the edge of the hand reads against each. Nails (joint lock, stylist): short, natural and unpolished, filed straight, with the right thumb cuticle slightly ragged. Skin finish (joint lock, stylist): matte, with no lotion or oil sheen, kept the same in every setup.
visual_identity_anchors: [macro] Build: a broad, square hand, 8.5 cm across the knuckles against a wrist about 6 cm across. Short, blunt fingers: the middle finger is about 7 cm, shorter than the palm is wide. Forearm about 26 cm around at its widest, with sparse, fine dark hair (#2A1E17) along the outer edge. This breaks the generator's long, tapered hand.
[macro] Skin: #6F4A34 on the back of the hand and forearm, with visible pores. Palms and fingertip pads are lighter, #B3886A. The back-of-hand hex is what reads in the widest counter shot.
[micro] Age texture: creased knuckles, darker than the surrounding skin (#4A2F20), on both hands. Two raised veins run from the wrist across the back of each hand.
[micro] Mark and asymmetry: a flat 4 mm mole (#3B2519) on the back of the right hand, 2 cm toward the wrist from the middle-finger knuckle. The left hand has none.

[micro] Writer's callus: a raised, matte pad about 5 mm across, a shade lighter than the finger (#86624A), on the thumb side of the right middle finger at the top joint, where a pen rests. It reads in the B1-B3 close-ups.

looks.garment_silhouette: Closet: mid-price, bought once and kept. She spends on her work coat, boots and paper, and skimps on house clothes, which are retired knits and old sleepwear. The idea: she is not dressed for anyone yet. At 7:00 she is in house clothes, and her work coat and boots are still by the door, so the look itself says the day hasn't claimed her (Route R1). The coat is backstory only; nothing is added to the set. Story: a weekday at 7:00, early November 2026 (ASSUMED). About 6 °C outside and 19 °C in the kitchen while the radiator warms up (ASSUMED), so she wears wool over a tee, trousers to the floor and socks, with ankles covered and shoes by the door. Head to toe: (1) crewneck pullover, hem at the hip bone; sleeve ends in the lower third of the forearm, 7 cm above the wrist bone at rest, 9 cm reaching; (2) short-sleeve crew tee under it, hem 3 cm below the pullover hem; (3) elastic-waist sleep trousers, full length, hem resting on the top of the foot; (4) crew socks to mid-calf; (5) no footwear. Older than the story: the pullover. She bought it around 2020. Two winters ago a 60 °C wash felted it and shrank the sleeves off her wrists, which made it her kitchen sweater, with nothing to push up before the pour. It is her one real detail (taste notes: 'one real detail... only this person would have') and the only garment the viewer sees (taste notes: 'Hands before faces'). Duplicates: use untreated, non-superwash 100% merino, because superwash will not felt. Start from a 12-gauge single-jersey crew one size up, give it one 60 °C wash and one tumble dry, and add a second dry only if it is still short of the numbers. Test one sample first, because shrink varies by yarn. Make 3, since a splash during the pour means a swap. Finished sizes, measured flat (ASSUMED from her 167 cm casting spec): sleeve 52 cm from shoulder seam to cuff edge; body 58 cm from the shoulder at the neck to the hem; chest 96 cm; cuff circumference 20 cm (her forearm girth 7 cm above the wrist bone, about 19 cm, plus 1 cm ease). The fitting resets these on the hero so the cuff lands 7 cm above the wrist bone with her hand flat on the counter. Every duplicate then matches the hero's measured numbers within ±0.5 cm. evidence.specificity: Every garment is listed head to toe with its landmark, fiber, weight, hex and ease. Even the garments that never appear on screen are specified: "Trousers: mid rise, 8 cm hip ease, full break, back hem 1 cm off the floor." Generation and storyboard can work from this without asking anything. The one gap is the pill lock (note 1), which names a frame the pills are not in.

cues.description: Room tone for Nora's kitchen in a small city flat at 7 a.m., heard close. What you hear: the low, steady hum of the fridge compressor off screen behind camera, and a thin wash of street traffic through a closed window, far off, with no horns or sirens. What's absent, and why: no birdsong (the dawn cliché). No neighbours' voices and no TV or radio, because nothing else in the room asks anything of her and there's no background speech to clear. No clock tick, because the phone's 7:00 is the only clock. It runs unbroken across every cut at one level and never drops to digital silence. The script's 'silence' is this room tone on its own, in two places: B1 1.25-1.50 s, continuing into B2 to 1.70 s, and B4b 9.85-11.00 s, continuing into B5 to 11.40 s. Arc: the loudest moment is the B4b rattle, 9.20-9.85 s, the face-down buzz with the glass flat on the wood (SND-D01-006). The quietest is room tone alone straight after it, B4b 9.85-11.00 s, continuing into B5 to 11.40 s, where the refusal lands. Sound never carries story information that muted viewers would miss: the 7:00 screen, the edge glow and the cards tell the story, and sound only adds to it. Feeds loop, so the level at 15.0 s matches 0.0 s and the loop runs cleanly into the B1 buzz. The generated clips' native audio is muted throughout. All sound is built in post.

assumptions: No frame rate was given, so 24 fps is assumed. Frames are round(seconds × 24) and must be recomputed if the edit runs at another rate. Picture-led points move with the edit (±2 frames). The B4b buzz is sound-led, so the picture's glow conforms to it.

Every window is labelled with the beat it sits in. Where room tone runs across a cut, it is written as '<beat> start-end s, continuing into <next beat> to X s'. Only the labels changed from the last version: every time and frame is the same.

The script's B4b 'One phone buzz rattling against the wood' and the route's 'a phone buzzing once' are read as one notification made of two pulses. Phone physics as a foley direction. Face-up, the phone rests on its camera bump and rocks, which gives a lopsided hum with a ticking rattle. evidence.specificity: Every sync point has a beat, a time in seconds and a frame. I checked each round(s x 24), and f2, f8, f30, f41, f62, f74, f89, f101, f103, f115, f158, f185, f193, f208, f221, f236, f250, f274, f295, f323 and f344 are all correct. Every sound names its source, material and perspective, so the editor and the foley session can work without a follow-up question. Example: "1.70 s (f41, picture-led, ±2): as the Solace dripper is lifted off the dish rack, its stoneware foot taps a coated-wire tine once, light and dry." The fixed hook is just as concrete: "The phone lies face-up, resting on its camera bump, so each pulse of the vibration motor rocks it. The result is a lopsided hum on the wooden counter, with a small ticking rattle each time the body taps the wood." Prior note 5 is addressed with a direction a recording session can follow: "use whole beans roasted within about two weeks and ground just before each take, place the mic a few centimetres above the cone, and record at least three pours."
evidence.distinctiveness: Sound now makes the refusal audible, not just visible, and that only works for this idea: "This time the whole glass face lies flat on the wood, so the buzz is flatter, wider and louder, and it rattles evenly through the counter with none of B1's rocking tick. It is 'harder this time' because she turned the phone over, so the flip can be heard." Two things nobody asked for also tie it to R1's clock: "No clock tick, because the phone's 7:00 is the only clock", and the cooling-kettle ticks spaced so "it never falls into a clock rhythm." Put this plan on another coffee spot and it breaks. The 7:00 phone, the face-up and face-down rhyme, the dish-rack tine and the product's own stoneware knock all belong to this film. It stops short of 10 because the room bed (fridge compressor, distant traffic) is ordinary city-flat atmosphere.
evidence.fit: The plan carries R1 exactly: sound instead of music, with the phone buzz as the turn. It also follows the script's no-music, no-VO, no-sting choices: "There's no riser, logo sound or button at 12.5-15.0 s." It works for muted viewers: "Sound never carries story information that muted viewers would miss: the 7:00 screen, the edge glow and the cards tell the story, and sound only adds to it." Prior note 4 is addressed openly. The plan says it reads the script's 'One phone buzz' as "one notification made of two pulses", gives the reason (the rhyme with B1), and adds single-pulse alternates for both B1 and B4b so the pair stays matched. It makes no product claims: "'Dense stoneware' is a sound-design direction and is never stated on screen. The verified facts appear only in the silent cards." The product is heard as a tool in B2 to B4a and is silent as the hero in B5 and B6, which follows 'The product is a tool, then a hero.' It stops short of 10 on one point: the script's B6 'kettle ticking as it cools, to the last frame' is changed to a last tick at 14.50 s, and the plan doesn't label that change as deliberate.
evidence.craft: All five prior notes were fixed. (1) The phone physics are now plausible: face-up it rocks on the camera bump, face-down the glass lies flat, and the session direction reads "records both orientations on that phone and counter: face-up on the camera bump, and face-down on the glass." (2) The beat labels stay inside their beats: "D01-B1, 0.10-1.50 s", "D01-B2, 1.50-4.00 s: room tone 1.50-1.70 s", "B4b 9.85-11.00 s, continuing into B5 to 11.40 s". (3) The rights have a named scope and owner, and none is claimed as cleared: "covering all media, worldwide, in perpetuity, including use beyond D01 (DTC product page, later cuts). Status: session and assignment pending. Owner: producer." The 001 cue adds a location release, and its library fallback has an assumed scope. (4) The single-pulse alternate is added. (5) The fizz has a recording direction and an in-world backup, and the plan says "The fizz is always recorded, never library." Cause comes before effect (kettle tip 4.20 s, then the stream lands 4.30 s). The ring-out is handled: "The last tick has died away by 14.50 s, so nothing is cut off at the last frame." Three small things keep it at 8 rather than 9. Two sync points in 004 are not marked sound-led or picture-led. The arc calls 9.85-11.40 s the quietest stretch while 001 holds room tone 'at one level', which could lead a mixer to dip it. And the 12-month library fallback would cap the soundtrack below the perpetual foley rights, which the plan doesn't flag.

assumptions: D01 at 24 fps (spec gives none; logged): 36+24+36+84+84+96 = 360 frames = 15.0 s. D02 stills: fps 24, 0 frames.
Full-frame-equivalent lenses; 9:16 on the 36 mm side (20.25 x 36 mm), 4:5 on 24 x 30 mm. Frame percentages are pinhole projections from the stated marks, about ±2%; confirm on the monitor.
No platform template: safe band 15-65% of height; the icon rail is taken as the right 12% of width from 40% to 90% of height (narrows v1's full-height 12%).
Marks: D01 phone at 40/255 (PD move requested), mug 27.3/295*, stack 27.3/311* in S1 and cheated unseen to 27.3/330 for S3-S4; D02-1 phone 48/268 (still only).

WIN-01 faces east at 7:00 in early November and the brick backs keep direct sun off the counter: ~5000K against a 5400K WB, ASSUMED; meter on the day. The hidden diffused unit outside WIN-01 is declared.
NORA 167 cm: eye 156, shoulder 137, torso half-width 20 cm or less; every clearance uses these figures.
Product size and glaze come from the world bible and are ASSUMED; no reference was inspected.
The 40 px pool pass mark is my hypothesis for 'readable'; the camera test on a 6-inch phone decides.

Taste notes followed: hands before faces (no face), no slow motion (all 100% speed), window never in frame and nobody gazing out, one real detail per scene (rack and cable, kettle scorch band, the ring, the face-down phone), tool then hero, ending on the product rather than a logo card. No taste note is broken; the all-locked grammar departs from the route (blocker 7).

blockers.issue: Route departure: R1 asks for a 'handheld-but-steady camera'; every shot here is locked. The reason isn't the cuts on action (those work handheld). It is: SH01's '7:00' composite locks to the glass without a track, and S1 keeps one grammar across SH01-SH03; at 100mm and 1 m, SH04 would turn handheld drift into apparent movement in the stream and bloom, the product's output; and the S3-S4 subtraction cut must register within 1%.
blockers.resolution: Director and Lucas approve the locked grammar, or approve handheld for S1 at the cost of a tracked '7:00' comp in SH01.

evidence.specificity: Every camera is placed with a plan position, a bearing, a tilt, a height in cm and a lens at a distance, and the numbers agree with each other when checked. "Camera C2 at 84/180, NORA's left, bearing 120° from the rack dripper, 35° down." paired with "40mm at 0.8 m. Lens 144 cm (46 cm over the rack dripper), which clears NORA's left side." works out to 65.5 cm horizontal, 46 cm vertical, 0.80 m. Action is frame-accurate against the treatment: "36f (9.0 s): phone lights face-down, edge glow, one rattle." A storyboard artist or a generator could build almost every frame without calling. Minor gaps: "Stopped down" gives no stop, and SH01 doesn't say which way the "10° off plumb" tilt goes.
evidence.distinctiveness: The hero's light and framing are built around a detail only this product has. "The pool is lit only by the window: one soft vertical window highlight on its frame-right flank, with no kicker and no retouch, because it is the hand-glazed proof." A competitor's evenly glazed cone breaks this shot. The story shots are just as particular: "A hidden flag takes the white plate 1 stop down so the cream dripper is the brightest detail in the hand." So is the ending: "Phone face-down and dark at 0-27% width, lower-left. Bare oak where the mug was." It stops short of 9 because it quietly loses S2's own real detail, the kettle's scorch band (see Fit).
evidence.fit: R1's structure, the product's role and every verified-fact limit hold, and no claims are added. But three things slip. First: "Every shot is locked off. This deliberately breaks the route's 'handheld-but-steady'; no taste note is broken." This settles a route departure in the assumptions instead of routing it to the director and Lucas. Second, the claim that no taste note is broken is false: SH04's 20 cm frame ("Spout enters top-right.") drops the kettle's scorch band, which is S2's one real detail and something the director's B3 acceptance check requires. Third, the readable-closing-moment must-include is still open: "The pool read at 65mm and 1.4 m (dripper about 26% of the frame width) is unverified, and the real rim diameter is unknown." There is no pass mark and no fallback.
evidence.craft: Most of the technique is right: "36+24+36+84+84+96 = 360 frames = 15.0 s.", screen direction holds, lenses exist, and cameras have distances. Checking the plan's own coordinates turns up four errors. (1) SH05: "Dripper, on the mug then on the ring, at 37-63% width and 45-60% height." From C4, the dripper sitting on the mug at 27.3/295 lands at about 69-95% width, inside the plan's own right-12% icon rail, during the last drip. The phone lands at about 72-86% height, not 64-72%. (2) SH04: "Stream at 15-50% of height, bed at 50-58%, mug rim below." That needs a drop of about 9 cm, but the world bible sets the spout 1-3 cm over the rim. (3) The light state changes inside a lock that has to register within 1%: SH05 says "Fill from the wall D and aisle bounce." and SH06 says "The aisle side is blacked so the gloss reflects only WIN-01 and wall D." (4) The hand double is used on several plates, but its release is not carried as pending.

notes.target: SH05 framing (and SH04→SH05 eye trace)
notes.note:
Recompute SH05 and give positions for each state separately. From C4 (136/236, 171 cm, 65mm, 9:16 on 20.25 × 36 mm):
- The dripper seated on the mug at 27.3/295 sits at about 69-95% width and 28-44% height for 0-24f, so the lift and the last drip (10-17f) play inside your own right-12% icon rail.
- The phone at 48/255 lands at about 72-86% height and runs from off-frame-left to about 31% width. That puts the B4b edge glow, the second refusal's only picture cue, under the bottom caption band.
- The eye jumps from SH04's cone at 38% to about 82%.
Fix within the camera: pan C4 about 10% of frame (about 2°) so the ring sits near 40% and the mug near 72%, which keeps the dripper on the mug inside 88%. Tilt down about 2°, and/or ask the PD to move the phone about 8 cm toward wall B, so the phone's lit wall-C and aisle edges sit above about 70%. Then state the ring, mug, phone and super-band percentages again, and where the eye lands across the 7.5 s cut.

notes.target: Blocker 4 / SH06 lens_intent
notes.note:
Put the closing read into numbers now, so the test has a pass mark and the shoot has a fallback. At 65mm and 1.4 m, the pool's 12 mm thickest arc is about 0.58 mm on the 20.25 mm width. That is about 31 px of a 1080 px master and about 2 mm on a 6-inch screen, and the 3 mm edge is about 8 px. Set the pass mark (for example, thickest arc at least 40 px) and list the fallbacks with their costs for the director:
- (a) Tighten the whole S3-S4 lock, which crops the mug and hand and reopens blocker 1.
- (b) A second locked body on the C4 axis at 135mm (two sizes, dripper about 60% of width) for B6 only. This loses the phone at the frame edge, so it is a director and script call.
notes.source: Brief must-include: 'A readable closing product moment'; craft brief: 'A cut to the same subject changes angle 30° or size two steps'; treatment S4 flag: 'Readability of the closing product moment'

notes.target: blockers (rights and route departure)
notes.note:
Add two blockers:
- (a) Hand-double release. The double is used in the SH01, SH03 and SH05 practical plates and in the SH07 still, and may feed generation for SH02. Name the source (the double's agent), the scope (D01 and D02 plates plus use as a generator reference), the owner (the producer) and the status (pending).
- (b) The all-locked grammar, as a route departure for the director and Lucas. The stated reason, that 'the cuts on action... need fixed frames', is wrong, because cuts on action work handheld. Give the real reasons: SH01's screen composite with one grammar per scene in S1, SH04's 100mm liquids, and the S3-S4 registration.

keep: The frame budget: 36+24+36+84+84+96 = 360 frames at the logged 24 fps, with frame-accurate action that matches the treatment's seconds (e.g. SH05 '36f (9.0 s)', drip at 10-17f).

One coordinate system for every setup: plan position, bearing, tilt, height in cm, and lens at a distance, all consistent with each other (SH02 40mm at 0.8 m from 84/180 at 35° down; SH03 65mm at 1.3 m; SH08 100mm at 1.1 m, dripper 44% of width).
SH01 as a neutral on-axis overhead, so '7:00' reads upright and resets the geography before the aisle-side coverage, tilted 10° off plumb to keep the rig out of the phone glass.
Screen direction and match points: SH02 exits right and SH03 enters left; SH03→SH04 cuts in two sizes on the same line, holding the cone at 38%/50%.
The SH06/SH08 hero light: window only, one highlight on the pool's frame-right flank, no kicker, no retouch, and the client's real unit shot practically, so the hand-glazed proof stays truthful.
The contrast arc 5:1 → 4:1 → 3:1, with flags taking the white plate and the gloss mug down so the cream dripper is the brightest detail.
Generator risks handled practical-first in every purpose line, at 100% speed, with no ramp and no added foam or steam.
The existing blockers routed to named owners: the C4 torso, the phone mark, the front arc 22° off lens, and the pool-read test.
